name: Reading Regulatory Filings
title: Reading Regulatory Filings
answer: Reading regulatory filings covers the documents public companies must file with securities regulators, including annual reports, quarterly reports, proxy statements, and material event disclosures. In the AI sector this means tracking how firms describe their models, their compute costs, their data sources, and the risks they attach to each. The work sits inside the wider practice of reading the market's language, where the same filing can be parsed for revenue, for litigation exposure, and for what management chooses not to say.

sections.body: Reading regulatory filings covers the documents public companies must file with securities regulators, including annual reports, quarterly reports, proxy statements, and material event disclosures. In the AI sector this means tracking how firms describe their models, their compute costs, their data sources, and the risks they attach to each. The work sits inside the wider practice of reading the market's language, where the same filing can be parsed for revenue, for litigation exposure, and for what management chooses not to say.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Filings arrive through regulator systems such as EDGAR in the United States and equivalent national repositories elsewhere, usually as structured text or HTML with tagged financial data. Analysts pull them by ticker or by filing type, then feed them into spreadsheets, document stores, or language models for search and comparison. This site's own tracking of 404 merger and acquisition filings and 517 company pages shows the scale at which such documents accumulate once a sector is followed closely.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core method is close reading against a checklist: revenue recognition, segment breakdowns, related party deals, risk factors, and changes in language from one period to the next. Readers compare a company's own claims with its audited numbers and with filings from competitors, suppliers, and customers. Language models speed up retrieval and summarisation, but the judgement about what a disclosure actually means still rests with a person who knows the business.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Filings are legal statements, and misstating them carries liability, so provenance matters: who signed, when it was filed, what was amended, and what was omitted. Material information must be disclosed, but companies retain wide discretion over how much detail they give, which is why risk factor sections are often broad and repetitive. Anyone using these documents should treat them as evidence to be checked against primary sources rather than as settled fact, and nothing here is legal, financial, or investment advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Disclosure rules are shifting toward more explicit treatment of AI: how models are built, where training data comes from, and what happens when systems fail. Regulators in several jurisdictions are consulting on climate style reporting for AI risk, and litigation tracked on this site, currently 152 active AI lawsuits, will shape what companies feel obliged to say. Expect filings to grow longer, more standardised in places, and more carefully worded everywhere.
